title: Horn Island, where serenity meets the mystery surrounding Nolan Wells’ death | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

The tides still rise and fall. Birds still migrate over its sparkling blue Gulf waters, and boaters still flock here on the weekends. But for one family, this uninhabited barrier island that once served as a toxic weapons site and endangered wildlife preserve has become a site of devastating loss and cripplinguncertainty.

Today, the island sanctuary lives a life of stillness and serenity, an escape from busy life on the mainland. But during warm-weather weekends, its white sand beaches are filled with boaters looking for a respite from the thick, sweltering heat of the Deep South.

Horn Island, some 12 nautical miles from Biloxi, exists in multiple realities at once: an isolated haven for wildlife, an outdoor playground of sorts and the place forever connected toNolan Wells’ death. The teen’s body was found on the shoreline days after a July 4 boating trip with a group of friends.

The case remains shadowed by competing autopsy results and the continued wait for toxicology results, leaving fundamental questions about Wells’ death largely unresolved: How did the young man become separated from his group? And what happened between the last time his friends saw him on the island and the discovery of his body, days later on the shore?

That uncertainty has reverberated far beyond his place of death, and in the absence of answers, has garnered national attention against the backdrop ofMississippi’s fraught historyof racial tension and violence.

After the law enforcement investigation, a Jackson County grand jury unanimously found there was no sufficient evidence to support charges and indict anyone in Wells’ death, Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath said.

That finding justisn’t enough for Wells’loved ones,advocates,lawmakersandathleteswho are determined to find answers about the teen’s final hours on theremote island.

Their ongoing insistence prompted Florida Rep. Frederica Wilsonto call for the National Park Service, which oversees Horn Island, to conduct a thorough investigation into the teen’s death, pursue all leads and keep his family informed of the findings. Even President DonaldTrump has saidhe is “looking at” the possibility of directing the FBI to investigate Wells’ death.

Horn Island, accessible only by private boat, is among just afew undeveloped barrier islandson the Gulf Coast, ideal in the warmer months for swimming, snorkeling, fishing and hiking, bird watching and camping in the cooler months.

The island may feel isolated, but geographically it’s part of something much bigger: Gulf Islands National Seashore, a national park that includes a dozen islands stretching160 milesacross Mississippi and Florida. Horn Island itself is about 10 miles long but only about a mile wide.

For most people who make the trek from Ocean Springs, Pascagoula, or Biloxi, the journeytakes about 30 minutes to an hour by boat.

The island’s remoteness and serenity is difficult to appreciate from looking at a map. The isolation sets in long before reaching the barrier island. As early as 15 minutes after leaving the dock in Biloxi, it becomes quite clear just how far – and fast – you’re removed from the mainland.

And because there are no facilities on Horn Island, once you’re here, you’re left to rely only on the supplies you take. The island lacks formal shelter and restrooms, and cell service is limited and often unreliable.

That seclusion makes Horn Island a haven for birdwatchers who come in hopes of catching a glimpse of a snowy plover or a least tern. But the stillness of the shorebirds’ paradise is regularly shaken by short-term visitors.

On busy summer weekends, the largely undeveloped shoreline can be lined with boats as its waters fill with visitors socializing, grilling, listening to music, and floating on inner tubes en masse.

Though popular with young adults, boaters of all ages often “raft up,” tying their vessels together in communal gathering spots where people can mingle from boat to boat with ease. On Mississippi’s Gulf Coast, boating is often ingrained in everyday life and often starts from a young age. State law allows childrenyounger than 12to operate a boat as long as they’re accompanied by someone at least 21 years old.

After the busy weekends come to an end, those crowds often dissolve, leaving the beach at peace and the water calm, both disturbed only by nature. Lingering visitors often find themselves alone with their thoughts accompanied only by the squawks of the shorebirds and thetranquil soundtrack of waves crashing against the coastline.

Unlike other national parks where rangers live and work on-site, Horn Island has no permanent ranger stationed there today. But that wasn’t always the case.

For much of Ben Moore’s 21-year career as a National Park Service ranger he was stationed on Horn Island, where he lived five days a week, according to a feature on his life inGulfLive. There, he would patrol the island, rescue stranded visitors, educate boaters and campers, help with wildlife releases and battle severe storms and, when tragedy struck, assist with the occasional recovery of a body from the water. The longtime ranger described his time working on the island as “a great experience” but one that was very uncomfortable, at times dangerous, always dirty but one of the best jobs he’s ever had.

National Park Service law enforcement rangers now patrol the island by vessel and foot.

When asked about the frequency of patrols, the NPS told CNN, “For operational and officer safety reasons” it declined to give specific schedules, staffing levels or information about deployments.

The long, slender island is home to sand, dunes, tidal flats and marshes. Horn Island was reshaped significantly in 2005, whenHurricane Katrinatormented its shores, eroding some parts so much it caused land loss along sections of the eastern end, the opposite area of where Nolan Wells’ body was recovered.

The island itself has a rich history that dates back centuries welcoming explorers, artists, fisherman, sailors and soldiers alike.

It acquired its name in the late 1600’s during the French exploration of the Mississippi barrier islands, according to theNPS,when a sailor lost his powder horn – a vessel in which to carry gunpowder. The sailor created a delay in the crew’s departure over the lost container and inspired the island’s namesake, “horn.”

Largely remaining untouched, the island has been interrupted only by brief periods of human presence.

During World War II, Horn Island housed a US Army chemical warfare station where toxic weapons were tested,according to the NPS. The Army carried out 23 tests between October 1943 and July 1994, which included experiments involving bombs containing botulinum toxin, a powerful poison that attacks the body’s nerves and can cause muscle paralysis, difficulty breathing and death, according to theCenters for Disease Control and Prevention.

Capitalizing on the islands relatively close remoteness, the US Army went back in 1946 for “Operation Hornblow.” Soldiers burned 133 leaking mustard bombs to destroy their toxic components in an isolated location. The bombs were part of a captured shipment of German explosives, the NPS said. Soil testing in 1947 found no traces of remaining toxic chemicals, the NPS said.

No trace of that military work can be seen nowadays.

Decades later, Horn Island transformed into a wildlife sanctuary when it served as a propagation site for the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s recovery efforts to save thehighly endangered red wolf. Horn Island became a “steppingstone between captivity and the wild,” which allowed red wolves to once live in a more natural, but still controlled environment before the animals were safely moved into wild, mainland populations,USFW has said. The red wolves are gone now, and fewer than two dozen remain in the wild.

The wildlife that calls the oasis home varies through its many different landscapes. Its maritime forest, lagoons, ponds, dunes and marshes provide habitat for alligators, brown pelicans, and raccoons, the NPS said.

Horn Island was among the Mississippi barrier islands affected by oil from the2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill, which lead to extensive cleanup and years of research monitoring wildlife and environmental impacts, according to the federal agency.

Recent testing again in 2013 found no traces of toxic chemicals, marking a stark contrast between Horn Island’s wartime past and its current status as a protected and preserved public land.

The sandy bottom remains visible through the light-colored shallow water along the shore, but the water quickly deepens offshore, turning into a darker, more opaque shade of blue. Stingrays, sea turtles, dolphins, and even some sharks can be seen from the shore.

Conditions in and around the Mississippi barrier islands can change quickly, according to the NPS, and have a history of powerful currents and drowning deaths, Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd told CNN in July.

Rip currents – or narrow channels of fast-paced, moving water that pulls swimmers away from the shore, sucking them into the water with no reprieve – can spike at any beach that has breaking waves, according to the NPS.

“The currents are strong out there — especially on that end of the island,” Lynd said of the area where Wells’ body wasfound face downin the water just off the shore on the northwestern end of the island. “There have been drownings out in the barrier islands many times over the years.”

On average, more than 100 people die in the USeach year from rip currents, according to theNPS.

But despite the potential danger the waters possess, deaths on Horn Island appear to be rare. A review of the park service’smortality dataset, which contains records from 2007 through 2019, found no reported deaths on Horn Island specifically, though several drowningshave been reportedthroughout Gulf Islands National Seashore.

At the stretch of the beach where the teen’s body was found, the shoreline is largely open with scattered sticks and hermit crabs peeking from holes along the water’s edge. On a calm day, the waves appear gentle. Small waves cross and build before they veer in different directions and eventually recede.

It remains unclear how Wells died and how his body wound up just offshore. But above the shoreline, the island now bears a physical reminder of the grim discovery. Two long white sticks, bound together with a frayed blue rope, form a makeshift cross perched atop a sandy dune. The memorial joins sparse patches of morning glory punctuated with its signature white flowers and dune grass, blades swaying with the breeze, as it overlooks the glittering water where Wells was found. Who placed the cross and when is unknown.

For decades, Horn Island has been known for its beauty, its serenity on a quiet day, and its energy on a popular one. In the wake of Wells’ death, it’s a place many are seeing for the first time, drawing their own conclusions about what happened on July 4.

But for those who loved the teen, the island may never look or feel the same again, forever tied to devastation, anguish and unanswered questions.
